newsitem.title: ITALY: Mideast faces terror surge without deal - Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Mideast faces terror surge without deal - Mubarak.

text.p: The Middle East could face a surge of "uncontrollable terrorism" unless Israel honours an accord to pull back its troops from the West Bank town of Hebron, Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak was quoted on Monday as saying.
"My principal fear is not war but terrorism," Mubarak told the Italian newspaper La Repubblica in an interview.
"That is our fear. Uncontrollable terrorism," he said.

"It would not hit only Israel but all neighbouring countries. Moderate Arab leaders who are working for peace will have enormous difficulty continuing down that road unless the other side responds to the desire for peace."
Palestinian and Israeli negotiators failed in talks on Sunday in self-ruled Jericho to hammer out a deal on a delayed Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, officials said.

The talks are stalemated over Israel's insistence that its troops be allowed to re-enter the 80 percent of Hebron slated to fall under PLO control if they are chasing suspected guerrillas in so-called "hot pursuit".

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has rejected any renegotiation of the Hebron accord, which was signed last year by a left-centre Israeli government ousted in May by conservative Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Mubarak said the "hot pursuit" issue was fundamental.
"It is not only a problem of dignity. It is that the population would rebel against the Israeli police and could take revenge and that would never lead to an improvement in the situation," he said.
Under the interim PLO-Israel peace deal, Hebron was to be handed over to Palestinian self-rule last year, but Israel delayed the transfer for security reasons.
Mubarak delivered the same message in an interview with Le Figaro, telling the French newspaper that he did not think war, between Syria and Israel for example, was likely.
"But violence, yes, and that is much more complicated to manage than war...How do you control terrorism? Is it the (Moslem) fundamentalists who benefit from tension?" he asked.

"(Those who benefit) are all those who are against peace, and there are many of them: in Israel as in other countries, there are some in Egypt too. There are many in Iran too who refuse the victory of peace," Mubarak said.
He said he continued to urge both Arafat and Netanyahu not to abandon negotiations. He told La Repubblica:
"I want to see the wheel of negotiations turn because a stall would be terrible. Unless Israel respects precise commitments, mistrust and suspicion will prevail.
"We are already in that climate," Mubarak said, adding that in Egypt, public opinion was "in revolt against Israel."
